content: Acute sinusitis typically begins following a preceding upper respiratory tract infection, which is most often caused by a virus. The viral infection damages the mucosal surfaces, creating an environment that allows bacteria to colonize. The most common bacterial pathogens involved are Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Staphylococcus aureus. Other bacterial contributors may include various species of streptococci, anaerobic bacteria, and, less frequently, gram-negative bacteria. Additionally, dental issues that affect the maxillary sinus can also lead to acute sinusitis. In some cases, acute sinusitis may result from fungal infections. These fungal infections are more commonly observed in individuals with compromised immune systems, such as those with diabetes, AIDS, or patients on immunosuppressive therapy following organ transplantation. Fungal sinusitis can be life-threatening in these populations. For instance, in individuals with type I diabetes, ketoacidosis can predispose them to sinusitis caused by Mucormycosis, a severe fungal infection. Chronic sinusitis, on the other hand, represents a complex group of conditions characterized by persistent inflammation of the sinuses. The etiology is multifactorial and may involve allergic reactions, environmental irritants such as dust or pollution, bacterial infections, or fungal involvement (which may be allergic, infectious, or reactive in nature). Non-allergic factors, such as vasomotor rhinitis, can also contribute to chronic sinus issues. The symptoms of chronic sinusitis include nasal congestion, facial pain, headaches, fever, general fatigue, thick green or yellow nasal discharge, a sensation of facial fullness that worsens when bending forward, and aching in the teeth. In rare cases, chronic sinusitis can lead to anosmia, which is the loss of the ability to smell. Occasionally, chronic maxillary sinusitis may arise from the spread of bacteria originating from a dental infection. Efforts have been made to standardize the classification of chronic sinusitis. The American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery, in collaboration with the Sinus and Allergy Health Partnership, has categorized chronic sinusitis into two primary subtypes: chronic sinusitis without nasal polyps and chronic sinusitis with nasal polyps (also referred to as chronic hyperplastic sinusitis). Recent research has identified the presence of eosinophils in the mucosal lining of the nasal and paranasal sinuses in many patients with chronic sinusitis. This has led to the term Eosinophilic Mucin Rhinosinusitis (EMRS). While EMRS may be associated with an allergic response, in many cases, no clear allergic trigger can be identified, leading to further classification into allergic and non-allergic EMRS subtypes. The role of fungi in chronic sinusitis remains a topic of ongoing debate. Fungi are frequently found in the nasal cavities and sinuses of individuals with sinusitis, but they are also present in healthy individuals. It is not yet fully understood whether fungi play a definitive role in the development of chronic sinusitis, and if so, what distinguishes individuals who develop the condition from those who do not.
